intro: A senior in Pilsen asks why her neighborhood still carries the name of a Czech city when most of the Czech families left decades ago. A search engine hands her one true paragraph that answers nothing. Twelve sources later, she has a question that changed shape, a folder of notes with page numbers, a grid where the sources argue with each other, and an eleven-page paper she can defend line by line. Then she has twelve minutes at the front of a room, and the first hand that goes up belongs to someone who read her paper and found the thing she cut.

This capstone unit puts together everything the course has built. Chapter one is the research paper, from a question worth a semester to a plan that protects revision, from library databases and articles that fight back to a synthesis grid, a long argument with rooms, MLA and APA, quotation and paraphrase done honestly, drafting in stages, a reader with a pencil, and the integrity that lets a stranger trust every line. Chapter two is the defense: a talk built for the ear, evidence on a screen, timing that fits, a question bank, the four-move answer to a hard challenge, discussion that builds, listening that judges the argument, feedback with an address, and an honest look back at how far you have come.

By the end you will be able to ask an open, specific, arguable question and go looking; find and weigh sources a reader can check; put twelve voices in conversation and add your own; credit every word and idea that is not yours; and stand behind the result out loud, conceding what is true and holding what the evidence holds. Those are not school skills. They are the habits of anyone who has to find out what is true and say so in front of people who are free to push back.
bigQuestion: How do you turn one honest question into an argument you can research, cite and defend in front of people who are free to disagree?

timeline.t: Write a first question, try to answer it in one sentence, and find the gap; that gap becomes the real question
Break the question into sub-questions and write a dated plan, putting the revision week on the calendar first
Search library databases with precise terms; read abstracts, then read the strongest sources in passes
Take notes in your own words with page numbers; mark every copied phrase with quotation marks
Fill the synthesis grid, sources across the top and themes down the side; write one sentence per row
Outline the argument as rooms, each answering one sub-question, with the strongest objection placed in the body
Draft the body one section per sitting, marking gaps in brackets; quote, paraphrase and summarize with citations
Write the conclusion, then the introduction; build the Works Cited or References list with hanging indents
Give the draft to a reader with three questions; reverse outline; revise from argument down to punctuation
Select one claim and three pieces of evidence for the talk; build one-idea slides and a reference slide
Rehearse out loud with a timer until there is slack; write the question bank and mark a cut point
Present, answer the hard question by restating, conceding, holding and marking the line; then reflect on what changed

words.d: the open, specific, arguable question a research paper sets out to answer; it cannot be settled by one lookup
the process in which other experts read and approve an article before a journal publishes it
combining sources by idea rather than by source, so their agreements and conflicts answer a question together
the one-sentence claim a whole paper argues for
the short note in parentheses inside a paragraph that points to an entry in the source list
restating a source's idea entirely in your own words and sentence structure, with a citation
words that introduce a quotation or paraphrase by naming the source: One historian argues
a one-line-per-paragraph summary made from a finished draft to reveal the structure it actually has
presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, whether on purpose or by accident, even with a citation if the words are copied
the one sentence a listener should be able to repeat after a talk is over
to admit that a specific part of a challenge is correct while holding what the evidence still supports
listening to judge an argument's claim, evidence and reasoning rather than the speaker's delivery

test.q: Which question has all three traits of a research question: open, specific and arguable?
choices: Why did two communities in one Chicago neighborhood each find reasons to keep a name that came from neither?
What year did the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal open?
Is history important?
How many murals are in Pilsen?
test.why: It names a place and a group, cannot be answered yes or no or by one source, and careful readers could answer it differently.

test.q: Dani's research plan put the revision week on the calendar before anything else. What problem does that prevent?
choices: Running out of sources
Choosing the wrong citation style
Revision getting squeezed into the last night because drafting slid late
Writing the introduction too early
test.why: When drafting runs late, revision is the stage that gets cut; fixing its dates first protects it.

test.q: Which source would a research paper treat as scholarly?
choices: An anonymous blog post with no date
A journal article by two named historians, checked by other historians before printing, with full notes
A comment under a video
A search engine's one-paragraph summary
test.why: Expert authors, peer review and full notes are the marks of a scholarly source.

test.q: On the first pass through a difficult journal article, the unit says to read what?
choices: Every footnote
The abstract, headings, first sentences and conclusion, to find the shape of the argument
Only the pages your teacher assigned
The whole article slowly, twice
test.why: The first pass is for the claim and the shape; close reading comes later, once you know where the article is going.

test.q: A paper summarizes Author A, then Author B, then Author C, each in its own section. What does the unit call this?
choices: Synthesis
Chronological order
A block quotation
A book report stacked twelve high, because the sources never speak to each other
test.why: Synthesis organizes by idea and brings sources together under each one; a source-by-source march does not.

test.q: Where does a paper's original contribution mostly come from, according to the unit?
choices: The writer's judgment where sources conflict, weighed with evidence
A source nobody else has found
The length of the Works Cited list
The formatting of the title page
test.why: Anyone can summarize twelve sources; only the writer can weigh them where they disagree.

test.q: Which in-text citation is in APA style?
choices: (Arredondo 42)
Arredondo, page 42
(Arredondo, 2008, p. 42)
[Arredondo 2008]
test.why: APA gives author and year, adding a page number with p. for a quotation; MLA gives author and page only.

test.q: A student swaps a few words in a source's sentence, keeps its order, and adds a correct citation. The unit calls this what?
choices: A proper paraphrase
A summary
Common knowledge
Patchwriting, which counts as plagiarism even with the citation
test.why: A real paraphrase changes both the words and the structure; the citation credits the idea but not copied wording.

test.q: Why does the unit say to write the introduction last?
choices: Because introductions are the least important part
Because you cannot introduce an argument you have not yet made
Because the outline replaces the introduction
Because readers skip introductions
test.why: The opening must present the thesis and the argument's shape, which exist only after the body is drafted.

test.q: Marcus, who knew nothing about Pilsen, found eleven places where Dani's draft lost him. Why was he a better reader than an expert would have been?
choices: An expert fills the gaps in a writer's logic without noticing them
Experts do not read drafts
He read it more times than she did
He was checking punctuation
test.why: A reader who does not know the subject sees only what is on the page, which is what a stranger will see.

test.q: Turning a twelve-page paper into a twelve-minute talk, the unit says, is not compression but selection. What does that mean?
choices: Talk faster to fit everything in
Read the paper's introduction aloud
Keep one claim and the three strongest pieces of evidence and drop the rest
Put the whole paper on slides
test.why: A listener cannot go back, so only the clearest, strongest points survive the move to a talk.

test.q: Which slide follows the one-idea rule?
choices: One quoted sentence in large type with its source beneath it
Six bullet points summarizing a section
Two charts side by side
A paragraph copied from the paper
test.why: One image, number or quotation keeps the audience's eyes and the speaker's voice on the same point.

test.q: A questioner says the argument leaves out money. The speaker agrees that developers used the name in the 1990s, holds that earlier decades still support the thesis, and says money is part of the later story, not the whole. This is which shape?
choices: Folding
Restate, concede, hold, mark the line
Stonewalling
Signposting
test.why: Specific concession plus a held claim, with the boundary named, is the honest answer to a hard question.

test.q: In evaluative listening, why is a confident speaker with a weak argument called dangerous to your judgment?
choices: Because confident speakers talk too fast
Because they never use slides
Because confidence feels like evidence and is not
Because they are always wrong
test.why: Delivery can persuade in place of reasoning; the claim, evidence and reasoning columns are the check.

test.q: Which comment is feedback the speaker can use?
choices: Great job, really interesting!
It was kind of confusing in the middle.
I think you should be more confident.
After the parish quotation you went straight to the next point; I did not know what to take from it. One sentence after the quote would fix that.
test.why: Usable feedback names a place, reports the listener's experience there, and suggests the smallest fix.

write.prompt: Dani's paper argued that the name Pilsen survived because each community found its own reasons to keep it; Jordan argued that money and developers explain more. Take a position on which account is better supported by the kinds of evidence described in this unit, and defend it as you would in front of a room.
tips: State a claim someone could disagree with: which account is stronger, and for which decades.
Use the unit's evidence: the parish history, the oral history, the 1960s displacement, the 1990s developer source, and say what each can and cannot carry.
Explain your reasoning in every paragraph: say why each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just that it does.
Concede what is true in the other account, then mark exactly where your claim holds and where it stops.
Cite every source you use, quote only when the wording matters, and end by naming what you still do not know.
